ip_top_stories.title: UK Government Opts Out of Its Previously Preferred Proposal on Copyright and AI
ip_top_stories.summary: The UK government has reversed its earlier preferred position on copyright and AI, stepping back from a previously favoured approach. Multiple sources, including Mondaq and legal commentary, note this signals continued uncertainty over how AI training and copyright will be regulated in the UK. The House of Lords has also weighed in, adding parliamentary pressure to resolve the issue.

ip_top_stories.title: SCOTUS's Cox Ruling Could Impact Publishers' Fight Against AI LLMs
ip_top_stories.summary: Publishers Weekly reports that the Supreme Court's ruling in the Cox case may open a new legal avenue for publishers challenging AI companies over large language model training on copyrighted works. The decision could affect how courts assess secondary liability in AI copyright disputes. Publishers and legal observers are watching closely for implications across ongoing litigation.

ip_top_stories.title: Researchers Challenge OpenAI Defence After Claiming ChatGPT Can Output Near-Verbatim Copies of Published Books
ip_top_stories.summary: Researchers have reportedly demonstrated that ChatGPT can reproduce near-verbatim passages from published books, directly challenging OpenAI's legal defence in copyright infringement cases. The findings are seen as significant in ongoing litigation brought by authors and publishers against OpenAI. The story is covered by International Business Times UK.

ip_top_stories.title: ANI vs OpenAI: Delhi High Court Reserves Verdict on Interim Relief in AI Copyright Dispute
ip_top_stories.summary: The Delhi High Court has reserved its verdict on an interim relief application in the copyright case brought by Indian news agency ANI against OpenAI. The case centres on whether OpenAI's use of ANI's content to train its AI models constitutes copyright infringement under Indian law. The ruling is expected to set an important precedent for AI and copyright in India.

ip_top_stories.title: Harlequin to Co-Produce AI-Generated 'Microdramas'
ip_top_stories.summary: Publishers Weekly reports that Harlequin has announced plans to co-produce a slate of AI-generated short-form video 'microdramas', marking a significant move by a major publisher into generative AI content production. The announcement raises questions about the role of AI in creative publishing and implications for authors and rights holders. No further details on licensing or creative credit arrangements were provided in the article.

ip_further_links.title: As AI Discourse Rages, Publishing Has More Questions Than Answers
ip_further_links.summary: Publishers Weekly surveys the publishing industry's ongoing uncertainty around AI, finding that despite intense debate, most publishers lack clear policies or answers on how to navigate AI's impact on rights, authorship, and business models.

ip_further_links.title: Australia Backs AI Licensing Under Copyright Rules
ip_further_links.summary: Australia has indicated support for an AI licensing framework under existing copyright rules, positioning itself in favour of remuneration for rights holders whose works are used to train AI models.

ip_further_links.title: Axios AI+DC Summit: Copyright Protection in the AI Era Will Be Up to the Courts, Industry Leaders Say
ip_further_links.summary: At the Axios AI+DC Summit, industry leaders said that resolving copyright protection in the AI era will largely fall to the courts rather than Congress, reflecting the current legislative stalemate in the US.

ip_further_links.title: Copyright in AI Prompts: Chinese Court Ruling on Generative AI and Originality
ip_further_links.summary: A Chinese court has issued a ruling examining whether AI-generated prompts can attract copyright protection, with the decision hinging on questions of originality — offering an important international perspective on generative AI and IP.

ip_further_links.title: The House of Lords Has Spoken on AI and Copyright – Here Is What It Means for You
ip_further_links.summary: An analysis of the UK House of Lords' recent intervention on AI and copyright, outlining what the recommendations mean for creators, publishers, and AI developers in the UK.

ip_further_links.title: How India is Trying to Navigate AI Copyright's Three-Body Problem
ip_further_links.summary: An analysis of India's complex challenge in balancing the competing interests of AI developers, rights holders, and the public as it considers how to regulate AI and copyright.

ip_further_links.title: Delhi HC Flags Legal Uncertainty Over Copyright in AI-Generated Songs
ip_further_links.summary: The Delhi High Court has flagged significant legal uncertainty over whether AI-generated music can attract copyright protection, highlighting a gap in existing Indian copyright law.

ip_further_links.title: Media Bosses: 'Australia Shouldn't Be Held to Ransom' by AI Giants
ip_further_links.summary: Australian media executives have called for stronger government action to ensure AI companies pay for the use of news content, warning that failure to act would leave publishers financially exposed.

ip_further_links.title: 'Manners for Machines': How New Rules Could Stop AI Scrapers Destroying the Internet
ip_further_links.summary: An examination of emerging technical and legal frameworks aimed at regulating AI web scraping, including proposals for standardised rules that would require AI crawlers to respect content rights.

ip_further_links.title: Is AI Software for IP Just Expensive Wrapping Paper?
ip_further_links.summary: IPKat examines whether current AI tools marketed to IP professionals genuinely add value or are largely repackaged existing technology at a premium price.
